title: David Nelson and Lee Collins fail with Russell; Red Allen shows how
summary: Neither Nelson nor Collins, who was meant to replace Allen, had the drive for Russell's band, and Red Allen's playing one night made Collins quit.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: I'd like to mention a few names to you, like David Nelson, King Oliver's nephew, who apparently tried to make it with the Russell band at one time. Were you there at the time when he was tried out?
Sure. He tried out and left. No, he couldn't make it at all. We needed a trumpet player with some get-up-and-go, you know. He didn't have that.
I think at one time Lee Collins was suggested for the...
No. They said he had it, but he didn't have it.

I think Lee was supposed to take Red's place, you know, and Red hadn't left the band when Lee showed up. One of them things, you know? So Lee is playing, you know, and not impressin' nobody. And Red comes walkin' in the place. So Red got up on the stand to blow some. Well, I mean, it was such a difference, night and day. Red knew what he was doing. And you know, Red was very arrogant anyway. He just knows he's the greatest. In other words, he was saying, "All right, down boy, down. I'll show you how it goes." Yeah, Red was very arrogant, and Red got up there blew... Hah! I don't think Red ever blew that much before in his life. And he looked at Lee, and he said, "Well, that's the way it goes." I think Lee was on the train the next morning going back to New Orleans.
Well, see, Lee Collins, he might have been a good trumpet player. I didn't know him. I didn't know that much of him. And for somebody to come right out of New Orleans

into New York City and sit in a band, and sit in a band that's pretty popular, you know, and he's got the leading part... I mean, that takes a lot of nerve. You know what I mean? I mean, you've got to know what you're doing. Because he didn't have the experience, for one thing. And I don't say he wasn't a good trumpet player. Naturally he's going to be nervous. But in Russell's band, they didn't give you no second chance. If you was nervous, then you had to go. Oh, they didn't care about who you were or what you thought you were or this-that-and-the-other, you know.
